reasons.reproducibility: Field trial in a disused UK canal with rotting straw; needs site access.
reasons.effectiveness: Summary says straw reduced filamentous algae but no numbers or controls seen.
reasons.time: Duration not reported; rotting-straw effects take months.
reasons.environment: Not reported; straw is biodegradable and retrievable.

reasons.reproducibility: Treatment of a whole UK supply reservoir at 25-50 g/m3 straw.
reasons.effectiveness: Productivity and cyanobacterial dominance 'significantly reduced', but numbers not seen.
reasons.time: Duration not reported; reservoir effects take months.
reasons.environment: 'No short-term deleterious impact' reported; more grazers.

reasons.reproducibility: Moored bales in an upland Scottish loch.
reasons.effectiveness: Cell numbers of main species affected but diversity not; no percentage.
reasons.environment: Bales served as invertebrate habitat; natural material.

reasons.reproducibility: Replicated limnocorrals inside a 1 ha pond need field access.
reasons.effectiveness: Negative: no consistent inhibition of filamentous or planktonic algae over 14 weeks.
reasons.environment: Decomposing straw caused low oxygen inside bales; zooplankton unaffected.

reasons.reproducibility: Lab bioassays are doable, but the reported field test used six 0.2-1.6 ha ponds.
reasons.effectiveness: Pond biomass did not differ between 4 treated and 2 control ponds on any date; lab response was species-specific (Anabaena unaffected, several algae stimulated).
reasons.cost: Straw is cheap, but repeating a six-pond season of sampling and Chl a work costs $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Pond trial ran May-September 1998, a full season.
reasons.environment: Straw is biodegradable, but liquor stimulated Selenastrum, Oscillatoria and Navicula.

reasons.reproducibility: Flask bioassays with straw and two Microcystis strains; bench scale with a sponsor for cultures.
reasons.effectiveness: Inhibition only after decomposition, only at 1-5 g/L (20-100x field rates), varied by strain and temperature, and sometimes in 2 of 3 replicates.
reasons.cost: Straw, flasks and a purchased Microcystis culture cost roughly $50-150.
reasons.time: Straw inhibition peaked only after ~1000 h (~6 weeks) of decomposition.
reasons.environment: Plant material that degrades; effect appears to work via H2O2, with no persistent residue.

reasons.reproducibility: Lab factorial culture test, but needs a purchased Prymnesium parvum culture and fish toxicity bioassays.
reasons.effectiveness: No barley straw extract dose (even 50x label) reduced P. parvum growth, density or fish toxicity; low dose raised growth ~10% at 30 C.
reasons.cost: Algal culture, commercial extract and fathead minnow tests cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: Endpoints were read after 23 days of culture.
reasons.environment: Extract is plant-derived with negligible nutrients, but it did nothing to lower fish toxicity.

reasons.reproducibility: Whole 240,000 m3 pond with 3 tons of straw on floating structures; not school-repeatable.
reasons.effectiveness: Aphanizomenon still dominated in June-July despite the standard 50 g/m2 dose; single pond with no control.
reasons.cost: 3 tons of straw, 150 rolls and anchored floating rafts cost $500-5,000.
reasons.environment: Pond stayed well oxygenated and straw is biodegradable.

reasons.reproducibility: 15 aquaria with reservoir water, sediment and 20 g straw each is a classic school setup.
reasons.effectiveness: Barley was only the comparison; camelina inhibited cyanobacteria more, and green algae were stimulated.

reasons.reproducibility: Flasks of lake water with 1% chopped barley straw; common materials and a clear bench protocol.
reasons.effectiveness: Triplicate flasks: no algal growth with barley straw vs ~10x rise in controls, and decomposed-straw extract cut Microcystis Chl a ~91% at every dose.
reasons.cost: Straw, lake water and flasks cost under $50.
reasons.time: Effects were tracked over 28 days, and the straw must be decomposed first.
reasons.environment: Biodegradable plant material, though wheat straw stimulated algae via nutrient leaching.

reasons.reproducibility: Lab tubes are simple, but the headline trial used nine 300 m2 earthen ponds.
reasons.effectiveness: Randomized pond trial (n=3 per arm): final Chl a 81-91% and cyanobacteria ~83% below controls, backed by lab bioassays.
reasons.cost: Straw is cheap, but nine ponds over four months of sampling cost $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Effect built up after a ~1-month lag and was clearest after 2-4 months.
reasons.environment: Treated ponds had doubled nitrate and a community shift to diatoms; Hydrodictyon was stimulated in the lab.

reasons.reproducibility: Flasks of Microcystis in natural water dosed with straw extract, counted by haemacytometer; bench scale.
reasons.effectiveness: All doses significantly cut cells and 10 mg/L gave 98% inhibition by day 8, but only duplicate runs and weaker effect in nutrient-rich water.
reasons.cost: Purchased Microcystis culture plus haemacytometer and flasks cost about $150-500.
reasons.environment: Plant extract with no persistent residue; non-target effects not assessed.

reasons.reproducibility: Review; the typical straw-liquor flask test uses common materials at bench scale.
reasons.effectiveness: Responses are species-dependent (inhibition, stimulation or none) and early field studies lacked controls and replication.
reasons.cost: Straw and jars for a typical liquor test cost under $50.
reasons.time: Straw must rot for weeks before inhibition, so results take one to three months.
reasons.environment: Biodegradable straw; may also help via bacteria competing for P and improved clarity.
